title: An ordinary morning (section 1)
hook: the Buddha dresses, walks for alms, eats, washes his feet and sits down

segments.voice: Yesterday, the turn, closed: three weeks of the Mahayana, a road wide enough for everyone. Your line: the great vehicle.

A man gets up. He gets dressed. He picks up a bowl and walks into town to ask for food. He eats what he's given. He walks back, puts the bowl away, washes his feet, and sits down. That's the whole first section of a great text of the Mahayana. No earthquake, no light from the sky, no gods arriving. Just a morning. For the next stretch of days, this path reads the Diamond Sutra, one short section a day. And it begins, on purpose or not, with chores.
screen: `DRESSED. BOWL. ALMS.` → `EAT. RETURN. WASH. SIT.` → `NO MIRACLE AT ALL.`

segments.voice: First, the name. In Sanskrit the sutra is the Vajracchedika. Max Müller's English translation titled it the Diamond-Cutter; people today call it the Diamond Sutra. A diamond: something hard enough to cut through other hard things. The sutra is going to cut. But not yet. Second, the scene, as the sutra sets it. It opens the old way: thus it was heard. The Buddha is staying near the city of Shravasti, in the Jeta grove, in the garden that Anathapindika gave, with a large company of monks. In the forenoon he puts on his robe, takes his bowl and cloak, and goes into the city for alms. He eats. He comes back from his round. He puts away his bowl and cloak. He washes his feet. He sits on the seat prepared for him, legs crossed, body upright, his attention set before him. Then the monks come and sit nearby. Third, what the sutra doesn't say. No deep thoughts on the walk. Nothing special about the food, nothing holy about the feet. Each act is simply done, then the next, at the speed of a person doing chores. Fourth, why start here. Some readers say this first section is already the whole teaching: before a word of wisdom is spoken, the Buddha shows it, by doing an ordinary morning completely and then sitting down. Others read it as the setting, the way any discourse opens. Either way, a text named for cutting begins with a bowl, a walk, and clean feet.
screen: `THE DIAMOND-CUTTER.` · `BOWL, ALMS, FEET, SEAT.` · `NOTHING SPECIAL IS SAID.` · `SHOWN BEFORE IT'S TAUGHT.` · then, large: `AN ORDINARY MORNING.`

segments.voice: If you can, do one small chore now, washing a cup, folding a shirt, wiping a counter, the way the sutra tells it: one act, then the next, nothing added. Feel the water's temperature and the weight of the cup, then put the thing away and sit, body upright, attention in front of you. If you can't get up, walk through this morning's first chore in memory, step by step.
Vajracchedika. The Diamond Sutra, the Diamond-Cutter in Max Müller's English, which opens on a plain morning of alms, a meal and washed feet. Today's word.
Your line: an ordinary morning. Wisdom, shown in a bowl and clean feet before it's spoken. Tomorrow, Subhuti asks.

howItsDone: The Diamond Sutra is chanted and studied in Mahayana communities, Zen among them; it opens with the Buddha's alms round, meal and quiet sitting.

chat.says: Why does a famous sutra on wisdom start with someone eating and washing his feet?
options: Some say it already shows the teaching: an ordinary morning, done fully.
Those were holy feet; the washing was a rite only Buddhas perform.
It's a mistake; the opening lines were added later by a copyist.
chat.meaning: The lesson gives two readings: some say the opening already shows the teaching, an ordinary morning done fully; others read it as the usual setting.

notes: Section 1 is paraphrased from Max Müller's Vagrakkhedika (SBE 49, 1894) rather than quoted, since the exact wording wasn't verified. Check the order of acts (robe, bowl and cloak, alms, eating, return, put away, wash feet, sit cross-legged, upright, mindfulness before him; then the monks approach).
The text gives a number of monks (1,250 in Müller); the script says 'a large company' to avoid an unverified count.
'Diamond-Cutter' is given as Müller's title, not as an etymology.
howItsDone says the sutra is chanted and studied in Mahayana communities including Zen; confirm.
